title: Predicting responses to psychedelics: A prospective study

claims.statement: In an online panel of US adults matched to the population on sex, age and ethnicity only (Prolific, October 2021; Simonsson et al., 2023), 613 of 2,822 respondents (21.7%) had ever used a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote or San Pedro). Asked once, looking back over their whole life, 362 of the 613 (59.1%) said they had never had a challenging, difficult or distressing experience with them, 143 (23.3%) rarely, 80 (13.1%) occasionally and 28 (4.6%) regularly or frequently: 41 in 100 at least once (editors' calculation). 28 (4.6%) said their ability to function had been severely impaired, and 55 (9.0%; printed 8.9%) that impairment had lasted more than a day, 21 of them (3.4%) more than a month (editors' sum), but the two impairment questions gave counts that do not agree (176 reported some impairment, 262 gave its length). In the days or weeks after their most challenging experience, 41 (6.7%) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others, including 9 (1.5%) attempts to harm themselves, and 16 (2.6%) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological help. 350 (57.1%) reported at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they put down to psychedelics, most often feeling anxious (36.1%) or difficulty sleeping (27.9%), but these questions, borrowed from meditation research, were not asked of people who had not used psychedelics or about times without them, so how many such symptoms would have happened anyway is unknown; 482 (78.6%) said they were glad to have used psychedelics. Challenging experiences were linked most often to LSD (by 31.5% of those who had used it, against 19.7% for psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT and 14.7% for mescaline, peyote or San Pedro), but how often each drug had been used was not asked. The 8 people taking lithium and the 16 taking another mood stabilizer at the time of their most challenging experience had higher odds of later harm thoughts or attempts (adjusted odds ratios 22.34, 95% CI 1.78 to 279.65, and 5.84, 1.40 to 24.34), estimates too imprecise, and too open to confounding by the conditions these medicines treat, to give a risk. In a self-selected online sample of people who had used psychedelics, 555 of 869 (64 in 100) said the experience they described had included a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort (Wood et al., 2024), which shows how much the figure depends on who is asked and how. In the one study that measured well-being before and after a planned psychedelic experience, 85 of 279 people (30 in 100) had lower well-being two weeks later, and they had not rated the experience as more challenging than the others (Haijen et al., 2018); with no comparison group, the fall cannot be put down to the drug. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Simonsson et al. (2023), of 613: never had a challenging experience 362 (59.1%); at least once 251 (40.9%, editors'); severe impairment 28 (4.6%); impairment over a day 55 (9.0%), over a month 21 (3.4%, editors'); harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%); sought help 16 (2.6%); lasting symptoms attributed to psychedelics 350 (57.1%, no comparison group); glad 482 (78.6%). Lithium (8 people) adjusted OR 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65), other mood stabilizers (16) 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34). Wood et al. (2024): 555 of 869 (63.9%) recalled distress in the experience they described. Haijen et al. (2018): well-being lower at two weeks in 85 of 279 (30.5%).

claims.statement: In adults planning to take a classic psychedelic on their own, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the one prospective study outside a laboratory (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07, a moderate association), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22, a small one). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences were associated with none. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions and set were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD lying in a hospital room, mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire just before the dose went with stronger effects on most self-rated scales but not with a bad drug effect, anxiety rated just before with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective online studies, as summarized by a systematic review rated critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience correlated strongly with it (surrender with mystical-type experience, r = 0.72; preoccupation and confusion with dread, 0.64 and 0.58), and in a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (adjusted odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions only (no sizes in the text). Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts adjusted OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94) (Simonsson et al., 2023).

claims.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the one prospective study found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults planning their own experience), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards as one yes-or-no item, was associated with no acute measure (0.02); the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (adjusted odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and none in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with neither (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating). Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts adjusted OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.
